# Overview

In this tutorial, we work through a complete multimodal regression workflow using **BayesCOOP**.

**BayesCOOP** is a scalable Bayesian framework for supervised multimodal integration with continuous outcomes. It uses group spike-and-slab double exponential shrinkage prior for joint feature/view selection and can optionally run a Bayesian bootstrap for uncertainty. For further details, see our [preprint](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.23.684056v1).

In this tutorial we: (1) load and preprocess a longitudinal pregnancy multi-omics dataset (immune + proteomics), (2) fit BayesCOOP with and without Bayesian bootstrap, and (3) feature selection sparsity.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 1. Package Setup

We assume **BayesCOOP** is already installed in your R library.

```{r load_BayesCOOP}
library(BayesCOOP)
```

Now we load the packages we are going to use in the rest of the tutorial: `BayesCOOP` (main method), `MultiAssayExperiment` (multimodal container), `dplyr` (data pre-processing), and `multiview` (Cooperative Learning).

```{r packages}
library(MultiAssayExperiment)
library(dplyr)
library(multiview)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 2. Load the Pregnancy Dataset

We load the pregnancy dataset from the [IntegratedLearner GitHub repository](https://github.com/himelmallick/IntegratedLearner) and convert it to `MultiAssayExperiment` objects for downstream modeling.

```{r load_data}
list_to_mae <- function(dat, y_col = "Y") {
  if (!all(c("feature_table", "sample_metadata", "feature_metadata") %in% names(dat))) {
    stop("Input list must contain feature_table, sample_metadata, and feature_metadata.")
  }
  if (!all(c("featureID", "featureType") %in% colnames(dat$feature_metadata))) {
    stop("feature_metadata must contain featureID and featureType.")
  }
  if (!(y_col %in% colnames(dat$sample_metadata))) {
    stop("sample_metadata must contain the response column Y.")
  }

  feature_table <- as.matrix(dat$feature_table)
  feature_metadata <- dat$feature_metadata
  sample_metadata <- dat$sample_metadata

  feature_metadata <- feature_metadata[match(rownames(feature_table), feature_metadata$featureID), , drop = FALSE]
  if (any(is.na(feature_metadata$featureID))) {
    stop("Each feature row in feature_table must have a matching entry in feature_metadata$featureID.")
  }

  modalities <- as.character(feature_metadata$featureType)
  assays <- lapply(unique(modalities), function(mod) {
    feature_table[modalities == mod, , drop = FALSE]
  })
  names(assays) <- unique(modalities)

  common_samples <- Reduce(intersect, c(list(rownames(sample_metadata)), lapply(assays, colnames)))
  sample_metadata <- sample_metadata[common_samples, , drop = FALSE]
  assays <- lapply(assays, function(mat) mat[, common_samples, drop = FALSE])

  MultiAssayExperiment::MultiAssayExperiment(
    experiments = assays,
    colData = S4Vectors::DataFrame(sample_metadata)
  )
}

## Load train data
data_train_list <- get(load(url(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/himelmallick/IntegratedLearner/master/data/StelzerDOS.RData"
)))

## Load test data
data_test_list <- get(load(url(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/himelmallick/IntegratedLearner/master/data/StelzerDOS_valid.RData"
)))

## Convert to MultiAssayExperiment
data_train <- list_to_mae(data_train_list)
data_test <- list_to_mae(data_test_list)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 3. Preprocessing

We remove metabolomics features since it’s not present in the validation set. Then we consider baseline samples only—training samples labeled with “A” and test samples labeled with “G1”—ensuring that all assays and outcomes stay synchronized across datasets.

```{r preprocess_data}
## Extract assays from MAE (feature x sample)
xList_train <- lapply(MultiAssayExperiment::experiments(data_train), as.matrix)
xList_test <- lapply(MultiAssayExperiment::experiments(data_test), as.matrix)

## Remove Metabolomics from training assays
xList_train <- xList_train[names(xList_train) != "Metabolomics"]

## Keep assays present in both train and test
shared_assays <- intersect(names(xList_train), names(xList_test))
xList_train <- xList_train[shared_assays]
xList_test <- xList_test[shared_assays]

## Extract response and sample IDs
y_train <- as.matrix(SummarizedExperiment::colData(data_train)$Y)
rownames(y_train) <- rownames(SummarizedExperiment::colData(data_train))
y_test <- as.matrix(SummarizedExperiment::colData(data_test)$Y)
rownames(y_test) <- rownames(SummarizedExperiment::colData(data_test))

## Selecting baseline observations from train and test data
pos_train <- grep("A", colnames(xList_train[[1]]), ignore.case = TRUE)
pos_test <- grep("G1", colnames(xList_test[[1]]))
xList_train <- lapply(xList_train, function(foo) foo[, pos_train, drop = FALSE])
xList_test <- lapply(xList_test, function(foo) foo[, pos_test, drop = FALSE])
y_train <- y_train[pos_train, , drop = FALSE]
y_test <- y_test[pos_test, , drop = FALSE]

## Convert to sample x feature data.frames and filter features
xList_train <- lapply(xList_train, function(foo) as.data.frame(t(foo)))
xList_test <- lapply(xList_test, function(foo) as.data.frame(t(foo)))
abd_thresh <- 0; prev_thresh <- 0.1
xList_train <- lapply(xList_train, function(foo) BayesCOOP:::filter_features(foo, abd_thresh, prev_thresh))
xList_test <- lapply(xList_test, function(foo) BayesCOOP:::filter_features(foo, abd_thresh, prev_thresh))

## Considering the common features between train and test set
keep_features <- vector("list", length = length(xList_train))
for(i in 1:length(keep_features)) {
  keep_features[[i]] <- intersect(names(xList_train[[i]]), names(xList_test[[i]]))
  xList_train[[i]] <- as.matrix(xList_train[[i]][, keep_features[[i]], drop = FALSE])
  xList_test[[i]] <- as.matrix(xList_test[[i]][, keep_features[[i]], drop = FALSE])
}

# Reconstruct MAE objects expected by BayesCOOP
data_train_processed <- BayesCOOP:::reconstruct_data(xList_train, y_train)
data_test_processed <- BayesCOOP:::reconstruct_data(xList_test, y_test)

```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 4. Fit BayesCOOP (Bayesian bootstrap enabled)

Here we fit BayesCOOP using `bb = TRUE` to enable Bayesian bootstrap–based uncertainty estimation. This step may take a while because it involves multiple bootstrap iterations, which can be adjusted through the `bbiters` and `bbburn` parameters. The output includes the posterior samples of the parameters and runtime.


```{r fit_bb_true}
set.seed(123)

## Fitting BayesCOOP
fit_BayesCOOP_bb_true <- BayesCOOP::BayesCOOP(data_train = data_train_processed,
  family = "gaussian",
  ss = c(0.05, 1),
  group = TRUE,
  bb = TRUE,
  alpha_dirich = 1,
  bbiters = 100,
  bbburn = 50,
  maxit = 10,
  warning = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE,
  control = list()
)

## Prediction
pred_BayesCOOP_bb_true <- predict(object = fit_BayesCOOP_bb_true,
                                            newdata = data_test_processed, family = "gaussian",
                                            bb = TRUE, warning = TRUE, verbose = TRUE)

## Calculating mean squared prediction error
mspe_BayesCOOP_bb_true <- mean((pred_BayesCOOP_bb_true$y_pred - pred_BayesCOOP_bb_true$y_valid) ^ 2)
print(mspe_BayesCOOP_bb_true)
```


------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 5. Fit BayesCOOP (Bayesian bootstrap disabled)

We also run BayesCOOP again with `bb = FALSE` to obtain posterior mode estimates via a faster MAP-style variant (without bootstrap-based uncertainty). All other settings remain unchanged.
```{r fit_bb_false}
set.seed(123)

## Fitting BayesCOOP with `bb` = FALSE
fit_BayesCOOP_bb_false <- BayesCOOP::BayesCOOP(
  data_train = data_train_processed,
  family = "gaussian",
  ss = c(0.05, 1),
  group = TRUE,
  bb = FALSE,
  alpha_dirich = 1,
  bbiters = 100,
  bbburn = 50,
  maxit = 10,
  warning = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE,
  control = list(rho = 0.5)
)

## Prediction
pred_BayesCOOP_bb_false <- predict(object = fit_BayesCOOP_bb_false,
                                            newdata = data_test_processed, family = "gaussian",
                                            bb = FALSE, warning = TRUE, verbose = TRUE)

## Calculating mean squared prediction error
mspe_BayesCOOP_bb_false <- mean((pred_BayesCOOP_bb_false$y_pred - pred_BayesCOOP_bb_false$y_valid) ^ 2)
print(mspe_BayesCOOP_bb_false)
```


# 6. Feature Selection / Sparsity Comparison

Finally, we count the number of **selected (nonzero) features** for each method to compare their **sparsity** and **selection aggressiveness**.  

```{r feature_selection_bcoop}
## Number of features selected for BayesCOOP with `bb` = TRUE
n_nz_BayesCOOP_bb_true  <- sum(fit_BayesCOOP_bb_true$beta_postmed!=0)
## Number of features selected for BayesCOOP with `bb` = FALSE
n_nz_BayesCOOP_bb_false <- sum(fit_BayesCOOP_bb_false$beta_MAP!=0)
```

For this particular dataset, both BayesCOOP variants achieved lower MSPE compared to their frequentist counterparts, with the Bayesian Bootstrap version producing a more parsimonious model. For an in-depth biological interpretation of the feature selection results, please check out our [preprint](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.23.684056v1).
